stories.headline: Odisha moves Supreme Court against Andhra Pradesh over rural poll notice in Kotia area
stories.deck: While all the 28 villages under Kotia Gram Panchayat remain in Odisha territory, Andhra Pradesh has been claiming its rights over 21 villages. Odisha challenged this in the Supreme Court in 1968 and the court asked both States to maintain the status quo in 2006
stories.bodyText:
The Odisha Government has filed a contempt of court petition against the Andhra Pradesh Government in the Supreme Court, challenging its notification to conduct panchayat elections in the disputed Kotia region in the state's Koraput district.
Odisha's Revenue and Disaster Management Minister Suresh Pujari said the petition was filed through the district collector of Koraput after the Andhra Pradesh Government issued a notification on October 10 to conduct Zilla Parishad and Panchayat Samiti elections in the Kotia cluster of villages in Odisha territory.
"We have filed the contempt petition in the apex court after getting approval from Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi," Mr. Pujari told reporters, adding that according to a 2006 Supreme Court order, both States are to maintain the status quo.
While all the 28 villages under Kotia Gram Panchayat remain in Odisha territory, Andhra Pradesh has been claiming its rights over 21 villages. Odisha challenged this in the Supreme Court in 1968 and the court asked both States to maintain the status quo in 2006.
However, Mr. Pujari said Andhra Pradesh has violated the Supreme Court order by notifying panchayat elections there. He said contempt proceedings have been made against the Andhra Pradesh Government, making the State Election Commissioner, Chief Secretary, the Collector of the district concerned, and other officers engaged in the election management parties to the matter.
"We will also pray to the Supreme Court to direct the Andhra Pradesh Government to refrain from such illegal activities in the future," the Minister said.
In 2021 also, there was tension between the two States when Andhra Pradesh held panchayat polls in the disputed region, prompting Odisha to file a contempt petition in 2022.
Now, the Andhra Pradesh administration has again notified local body polls in the disputed villages of Phagunasineri, Ganjeipadar, and Phatusineri, an official said.
Mr. Pujari said Kotia is an integral part of Odisha, and the State is taking legal and administrative steps to uphold its rights.

stories.headline: Students, farmers, civil society groups continue to protest against SIR, CEC
stories.deck: Hundreds take to the streets as Yogendra Yadav, Annie Raja, and farmers’ groups join protest; police say 20 detained, one FIR resgistered
stories.bodyText:
Around 500 protesters from students, youth, women, farmers, and civil society organisations, under the banner of ‘People Against SIR’ marched through Central Delhi on Friday (October 23, 2026), demanding the rollback of the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. The march was part of a series of protests held across the country against the exercise.
The Delhi Police said around 20 protesters were detained and later released, even as protesters claimed that around 50 were rounded up. Police registered at least one FIR against protesters for violating prohibitory orders under Section 163 of Bharatiya Nagrik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).
The protesters, carrying the national flag, banners, and placards, assembled near the Gol Dak Khana roundabout at the intersection of Kali Bari Marg and Bhai Vir Singh Marg, before attempting to march towards the Election Commission of India (ECI) headquarters. Ahead of the 1 p.m. protest call, participants gathered in small groups around Bangla Sahib Gurdwara.
Political activist Yogendra Yadav, Communist Party of India leader Annie Raja, and All India Kisan Sabha vice-president Inderjeet Singh joined the march. Representatives of student organisations, including the All India Students’ Association, All India Students’ Federation, Students’ Federation of India, Krantikari Yuva Sangathan and All India Democratic Students’ Organisation, also participated.
Addressing protesters, Mr. Yadav said the movement would continue despite restrictions on demonstrations, including the denotification of Jantar Mantar as a protest site.
“The protest will continue. If you shut down one Jantar Mantar, hundreds more will emerge. If you try to silence one person, people will not remain quiet. People and organisations may change, but the movement will go on. Until Gyanesh Kumar resigns, we will continue to protest,” he said.
Mr. Singh said the Samyukt Kisan Morcha (SKM) decided to support the movement after the protesters, particularly women, were manhandled during earlier demonstrations in Delhi.
“We are angry about what has happened to our young people, particularly the women protesters, who were pushed to the ground and had their clothes torn. Enough is enough. We will continue to support this movement until the SIR is scrapped, the right to vote is protected, and the right to protest at Jantar Mantar is restored,” he said.
Mr. Singh opposed giving police power via Special Executive Magistrates in proceedings against protesters, arguing that the arrangement concentrated too much authority in the hands of the police.
“Now they are the judge, they are the lawyers, the court itself is theirs, it is only natural that we will be declared the criminal,” he said.
Ms. Raja accused the Centre of using the SIR exercise to undermine constitutional safeguards and said the protests would continue until the CEC stepped down.
“The SIR is a tool being used by the Narendra Modi government to undermine the Constitution. The people of this country will not allow that to happen, which is why we continue to raise our voices. We have come very close to the CEC’s office today. Soon we will also reach there and ask him to get out,” she said.
“From Kashmir to Kanyakumari, and from the Northeast to Gujarat, people are organising their own Jantar Mantars. Even if the authorities restrict one protest site, people will find ways to make their voices heard,” she said.
Among those who joined the demonstration was Subhas Mishra, an information technology professional from Bengaluru, who came with his wife. He said citizens needed to participate in public demonstrations rather than confining political discussions to private spaces.
“I am here to support Prashant Bhushan, Abhijeet Dipke and everyone who believes in democracy. Discussions cannot remain confined to drawing rooms and WhatsApp groups. People must come out of their homes. Nothing will change if we only talk among ourselves,” he said.
“The way Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were kept in jail for a week was dictatorial. It is time for people to come out on the streets and exercise their democratic right to protest,” he added.
Barricades halt march
The protesters began marching towards the ECI but were stopped by multiple barricades and security personnel on Ashoka Road, around 500 metres into the march. They briefly sat down on the road as police personnel warned them about the prohibitory orders imposed under Section 163 of BNSS.
The police subsequently pushed the protesters back towards the main road, using whistles and repeated warnings about detention for violating the restrictions. As slogans continued, several protesters were taken away in two detention vehicles near the Gol Dak Khana roundabout.
Separately, the SKM said farmers held demonstrations at district and tehsil headquarters across the country, demanding that the SIR be scrapped and Mr. Kumar be sacked and prosecuted. Farmer delegations submitted memoranda addressed to President Droupadi Murmu through District Magistrates and Sub-Divisional Magistrates.
“In many places, police tried to stop the protests. Leaders were kept under house arrest from early morning, protesters were detained on their way, and prohibitory orders were imposed in Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, [and] Haryana, particularly [in] BJP-ruled States,” the organisation said in its statement. SKM also demanded that the Delhi Police must withdraw its order that removed Jantar Mantar as a protest site.
The October 23 mobilisation followed the formation of People Against SIR last week, after an emergency consultation in Delhi attended by representatives of more than 200 organisations. The platform brings together 145 civil society groups, farmers’ unions, workers’ organisations, and women’s and youth groups across 18 States.

stories.headline: FBI detains gangster Himanshu Bhau, India may get custody soon
stories.deck: Himanshu Bhau, a notorious gangster from north India, was recently captured by the FBI in Las Vegas. He has been wanted for a series of violent offenses, including multiple murders and extortion schemes that have plagued Delhi and Haryana. After escaping juvenile detention in 2020, he maintained his criminal operations through illegal networks.
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Himanshu Bhau, one of north India's most wanted gangsters, is learnt to have been detained in the US, after a four-year-long manhunt. Subject of a red notice from the Interpol, Bhau, a rival of Lawrence Bishnoi group, is wanted for multiple cases off shootings, killings and multi-crore extortions in Delhi and Haryana.
Bhau, sources said, was apprehended by FBI in Las Vegas/Nevada region following inputs from Indian agencies. He is likely to be handed over to Indian law enforcement agencies, who have been chasing him since 2022, in the coming days, sources said.
In his early twenties, Bhau is one of north India's most notorious young fugitives, heading an organised crime syndicate. He has been a headache for cops in Delhi, Haryana and Rajasthan with back-to-back killings, including three sensational murders in Delhi, this year.
Himanshu's major cirmes
"He belongs to Ritoli in the Rohtak district of Haryana and had got involved in crimes while still in school. He first entered police records in 2020 following a botched killing attempt involving a localized dispute in his native village," an investigator recalled.
Since he was a minor at the time of apprehension, cops detained him and sent him to a juvenile observation home in Hisar. However, his stay there was brief; he engineered an audacious escape from the facility, casting aside any prospect of rehabilitation and plunging headfirst into a career of violent crime that soon expanded far beyond rural Haryana.
Operating in close coordination with seasoned syndicates, including the Neeraj Bawana and Naveen Bali gangs, Bhau rapidly built a formidable network spanning Rohtak, Jhunjhunu, Sonipat, and the National Capital Region of Delhi.
As law enforcement agencies closed in on his local footprints, including a series of high-profile murders in his home district in March 2022, he managed to orchestrate an escape from the country.
"In 2022, he executed three killings in a span of 24 days in March. The same year, using a passport obtained through fraudulent documents, Bhau slipped across international borders, initially fleeing to Dubai before moving on to European safe havens like Portugal, from where he continued to remotely direct his syndicate," said an investigator.
Despite being a fugitive with Red Corner Notices and heavy cash rewards issued by multiple police jurisdictions and the National Investigation Agency, he leveraged encrypted messaging applications to command local shooters.
He is suspected to have reached US through the "Dunkey Route" in late 2024-early 2025.
His syndicate has claimed responsibility for a string of high-profile shootings, extortions, and contract killings that terrorised businessmen and shook law enforcement.
Among his syndicate's most brazen operations was the daring killing of a rival at a prominent fast-food chain outlet in West Delhi's Rajouri Garden.
His network has also targeted commercial establishments, unleashing dozens of rounds of gunfire at car showrooms in Naraina and Tilak Nagar alongside multi-million rupee extortion demands directed at builders, real estate developers, and local traders across Delhi-NCR.

stories.headline: Typhoon Champi sweeps past Taiwan, one dead and 500 injured
stories.bodyText: Taipei: Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person and injuring more than 500, downing trees and severing power, as it continues to weaken and head north towards the Chinese coast. At one point a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the Pacific this year, Champi is weakening though still packing gusts of around 126 kph (78 mph) near its centre, according to Taiwan's Central Weather Administration (CWA). .Political affirmative action? Look to Taiwan. The storm was about 150 km (93 miles) east of Taiwan, the CWA said, having glanced the island's northeast coast in the early hours of Saturday. The storm's forecast track shows it is now turning north toward the Chinese coast and eventually move into southern Japan. Taiwan's fire department said the death toll remaining at one, a man swept away by waves from the island of Liuqiu, with 527 injuries during the heavy wind and torrential rain. Taipower said at one point more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, though most had been reconnected. The transport ministry said 242 flights were cancelled, though that was an improvement from Friday when the number was almost 1,000. In the capital Taipei, there were downed trees and on-off squally rain showers. .Taiwan: Rare police raid on Taipei gay bar sparks angry protest. A swathe of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second day of office and school closures on Saturday. Taiwan is generally very well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike in autumn too.

briefs.headline: Local humanitarian ceasefire with Russia will start on October 27, says negotiator
briefs.deck: Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators reached a deal to provide humanitarian assistance in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine
briefs.bodyText:
Ukraine's top negotiator involved in a humanitarian mission led by U.S. first lady Melania Trump told The Associated Press that a local ceasefire with Russia will start Tuesday (October 27, 2026) — two days before the mission begins — and last several days.
Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators reached a deal on Friday (October 23, 2026) to provide humanitarian assistance in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, in the war-divided region of Kherson in southern Ukraine.
Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian ombudsman and his country's chief negotiator in the talks, said the ceasefire would take effect across the Kherson region and neighbouring areas essential to the operation. He added that the initiative could act as a model for future humanitarian missions.
The White House said Melania Trump had initiated discussions after learning about the situation during an event she hosted during last month's UN General Assembly session. It said she and a representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the ceasefire. Russian officials also confirmed the arrangement.
Mr. Lubinets earlier on Friday (October 23, 2026) thanked Melania Trump for her involvement and said the deal would be tough to accomplish. He said the agreement calls for a ceasefire, followed by the delivery of much-needed humanitarian aid. Lastly, civilians will be allowed to leave Oleshky, he said in a video message posted online.
"The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement," Mr. Lubinets said.
The removal of mines comes first
Mr. Lubinets said the operation would involve removing mines on the way to Oleshky before the physical delivery of humanitarian aid and the arranging of evacuations.
He gave no further details on how the ceasefire or the aid mission would be monitored or implemented, citing the sensitivity of the negotiations. He declined to comment when asked if Melania Trump would travel to Ukraine but described her involvement as invaluable.
"When Melania Trump learned about the situation in Oleshky, the negotiation process began under her coordination," he said. "For several weeks, we discussed many questions, initiatives and ideas. We established new approaches, mechanisms and tools to do everything possible to help civilians in Oleshky survive."
Russia's chief of the general staff, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, said Russian forces "will cease fire on the Kherson axis" starting at 4 am on Tuesday in Moscow "in connection with the humanitarian operation near Oleshky". Russian forces will also carry out "engineering reconnaissance" and ensure "safe movement of the humanitarian convoy" into the city, Mr. Gerasimov said.
Russia's human rights ombudswoman, Yana Lantratova, confirmed on Friday (October 23, 2026) that Melania Trump had brokered an agreement on "organising a humanitarian mission" in Oleshky. Lantratova, who said she participated in negotiations, said providing such assistance is Russia's priority.
The first step will be to clarify what people need and organise the delivery of food, medicine, hygiene products and other essentials, Lantratova said in an online statement. Safe passage will be guaranteed for anyone who wants to leave the combat zone, she said, adding that it will require abiding by the ceasefire and creating safe conditions for humanitarian vehicles.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow was grateful to the First Lady. He said Russian President Vladimir Putin and President Donald Trump had recently discussed the effort.
Mr. Peskov said "those who want to leave it would be able to do so". He would not say whether they would be taken to Russia- or Ukraine-held territory. He also demurred when asked how long the evacuation will last, saying only it would most likely take several days.
Saving children is the First Lady's focus, says President
Ms. Melania Trump has made helping children in conflict zones one of her signature issues in her husband's second term. She hosted a UN Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year, and last year wrote Putin about efforts to reunite families with children who have been displaced by the war. She has helped reunite nearly three dozen children, according to her senior adviser, Marc Beckman.
"What she wants to do is save children, and that is her focus," the President said about his wife during a question-and-answer exchange with journalists at the White House.
Mr. Beckman portrayed the First Lady's work on the ceasefire as an extension of her efforts to help reunite Russian and Ukrainian children with their families after they were separated by Russia's war against Ukraine.
Tensions between Washington and Kyiv are rising
The development comes as tensions have increased to new highs between the Trump administration and Ukraine's government. Kyiv has faced restrictions on the satellite internet system it relies on to knock down Russian attacks, with Mr. Trump and other top U.S. officials sending mixed messages about who was responsible for throttling the Elon Musk-made Starshield system.
Mr. Trump also recently waived new Russia sanctions, reached an agreement with Russia to import diesel fuel and pushed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make a deal to end the war that Russia began in February 2022. In renewed efforts to revive the peace process, Mr. Trump Envoy Steve Witkoff travelled to Norway this week for talks with Mr. Zelenskyy before meeting Mr. Putin in St Petersburg, Russia.
Mr. Zelenskyy did not mention the ceasefire in Oleshky during a remote appearance at the Hudson Institute, a Washington think tank. He did note that American Patriot missile interceptors were still on hold and Starshield and Starlink speed limits were still in place.
He also spoke of the importance of the United States to renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war, including a possible joint meeting with Trump and Putin.
The situation in Oleshky is dire
Food and medical supplies have been scarce for months in Oleshky, which sits on the Dnipro river that separates Ukrainian forces from the city's Russian occupiers. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Roads leading from town are mined and dotted with burned-out cars. Drones buzz overhead.
Once a city of about 24,000 residents, Oleshky was captured by Moscow's forces on the first day of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned, and its infrastructure damaged. In June 2023, floodwaters inundated the city after the Kakhovka dam collapsed from an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed.
Those left in the city along Ukraine's southeastern front face death from hunger or disease as another harsh winter looms. Ukraine has appealed repeatedly for a local ceasefire to organise evacuations. Russia, as the occupying power, is obligated by international law to ensure civilians under its control have what they need to survive.

briefs.headline: Trump says U.S. will 'take care of Cuba' on its way back from Iran
briefs.deck: Mr. Trump predicted last month the U.S. and Cuba would reach an agreement and that he did not ‌think military action would be necessary
briefs.bodyText:
President Donald Trump said on Friday (October 23, 2026) the United States would take care of Cuba after dealing with Iran and would send Secretary of State Marco Rubio to finish the deal.
"We'll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran ... then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal," Mr. Trump told a rally in Florida.
Mr. Trump predicted last month the U.S. and Cuba would reach an agreement and that he did not think military action would be necessary.
The Trump administration has previously stated its goal is to change Cuba's communist government.
A U.S.-imposed oil blockade implemented earlier this year has put Cuba under severe strain as it contends with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.
Washington has maintained an embargo on Cuba for more than 60 years and the Trump administration has been stepping up pressure on Havana after the U.S. military in January seized then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in a deadly raid.
Cuba's Foreign Minister told the UN General Assembly last month Cuba would always be open for dialogue with Washington.

briefs.headline: Trump lifts some Canada tariffs ahead of midterms
briefs.deck: The change could help Senator Susan Collins, who faces a strong challenge from a Democrat in Maine, a U.S.-Canada border state hit hard by Donald Trump’s trade war
briefs.bodyText:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration lifted some tariffs on Canadian imports on Friday (October 23, 2026), two weeks ahead of midterm elections, after a vulnerable Republican candidate said she’d lobbied for the change.
The easing of tariffs will apply to products including “plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment,” the White House said in a statement.
The change could help Senator Susan Collins, who faces a strong challenge from a Democrat in Maine, a U.S.-Canada border state hit hard by Mr. Trump’s trade war.
She posted on social media that she had “secured” the exemptions for “products crucial to Maine’s agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers.”
Democrats are targeting Ms. Collins’s seat in their attempt to win control of Congress from the Republicans in the November 3 midterms.
U.S.-Canada trade
The economies of the United States and Canada are heavily interconnected, with roughly 70% of Canada’s exports heading to the United States.
Tensions between the North American neighbours have been high since trade talks broke down in August, with Mr. Trump imposing a slew of new tariffs in response.
Friday’s (October 23, 2026) action lifts tariffs on certain goods, but imposes levies on new ones, including carpets, certain valves and waste products, the White House said. The new measures will take effect on October 30.
“The Canadian government takes note of these recent tariff measures adopted by the United States,” Dominic LeBlanc, Ottawa’s Minister in charge of U.S.-Canada trade, said in a statement to AFP.
“While evaluating these recent measures, Canada remains ready to work together in a constructive and good-faith manner” with the U.S., he added.
Ms. Collins said many farmers in her state “rely on specialised equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense.”
Previous Trump levies on autos, steel, aluminium, and lumber have hit Canada hard, forcing job losses and stunting growth. Canada has entered a technical recession this year after two consecutive quarters of economic contraction.
Mr. Trump’s tariffs, enforced after the talks broke down, impacted around $20 billion worth of goods, or 5.5% of Canadian exports to the United States, targeting products ranging from hockey sticks to cement.
Since taking power in his second term, Mr. Trump has upended the global trade order by imposing wide-ranging tariffs on friends and foes alike, saying that other countries have been taking advantage of the United States.
He has also explicitly tied some threatened tariffs to political or foreign policy objectives.

briefs.headline: IndiGo extends cancellation of Saudi flights as regional tensions escalate: Indian mission
briefs.deck: IndiGo has extended the cancellation of its flights to and from Saudi Arabia as regional security concerns escalate, with Riyadh routes halted until October 31, 2026 and Jeddah, Dammam, and Madinah routes until October 27, 2026, the Indian Embassy in Riyadh said.
briefs.bodyText:
Indian airline IndiGo has extended the suspension of its flights to and from Saudi Arabia amid escalating security concerns in the region, said the Indian Embassy in Riyadh on Friday (October 23, 2026).
“IndiGo flights to and from Riyadh will remain cancelled until 31 October 2026 [inclusive], while flights to and from Jeddah, Dammam and Madinah will remain cancelled until 27 October 2026 [inclusive],” the mission said in a post on X.
The latest extension of flight cancellations follows a series of Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday (October 21, 2026), including a strike on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam that killed an Indian national and injured two others, and a separate attack on Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield that injured another Indian national.
IndiGo joins Indian carriers that have already halted operations following a series of Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting key infrastructure. Air India and Air India Express have suspended services until October 24, while Akasa Air has extended its cancellations until October 27.
.
"Indian nationals requiring urgent departure may consider transiting via Bahrain, Kuwait, or Qatar, subject to obtaining the necessary visas," the Indian mission said earlier.
The flight disruptions have also affected Indian Umrah pilgrims, prompting the Ministry of External Affairs to coordinate with airlines and tour operators to facilitate their early return.
MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the Indian Embassy in Riyadh and the Consulate General in Jeddah were engaging with airlines and tour operators to arrange the return of the remaining affected pilgrims at the earliest.
The missions in Saudi Arabia have established 24-hour control rooms to help Indian nationals. They are also issuing regular advisories in view of the prevailing security situation.
An earlier attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on October 10 killed an Indian national and injured several others, prompting the Indian Embassy to issue safety advisories for the Indian community.
The embassy has urged Indian nationals to remain alert, follow instructions issued by Saudi authorities and move to a safe place inside a building in the event of an aerial attack.
It has also warned them against filming or sharing images and videos of interceptions or impact sites, citing possible legal consequences under Saudi law.
Saudi Arabia is home to approximately 2.74 million Indian nationals, who work across various sectors and form an important link between the two countries.

briefs.headline: Nuclear power could more than triple by 2060, UN agency says
briefs.deck: Rafael Grossi says in the IAEA's annual report that nuclear power will be driven by electrification, data centres powered by artificial intelligence and "technology companies' appetite for reliable, carbon-free power"
briefs.bodyText:
The head of the UN nuclear agency, Rafael Grossi, said on Friday (October 23, 2026) that he expects the use of nuclear power could more than triple by 2060.
Mr. Grossi said in the International Atomic Energy Agency's annual report to the UN General Assembly that this will be driven by electrification, data centres powered by artificial intelligence and "technology companies' appetite for reliable, carbon-free power".
Nuclear energy is seen by a growing number of countries as key to improving their energy security, he said, stressing that it is on par with solar energy and "safer than every other option".
"In 2025, more than 400 operating reactors in more than 30 countries produced 10% of global electricity and a quarter of its low-carbon electricity," the IAEA director-general said. "More than 60 new reactors are under construction, and the projections for future nuclear capacity have shifted dramatically upward."
In addition to the growing use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, Mr. Grossi spoke about the nuclear programmes in Iran and North Korea, the "unprecedented threats to nuclear safety" from the war in Ukraine, and worrying reports that other countries he did not name are talking about acquiring nuclear weapons.
On Iran, whose nuclear sites were struck by the U.S. last year before the U.S. and Israel launched a war on February 28, Mr. Grossi told UN member nations that the necessary technical work for a diplomatic agreement has been done.
"I call on the parties to redouble their efforts towards agreeing a diplomatic solution that includes the IAEA's indispensable verification role, without which no agreement can be sustainable," he said. "IAEA inspectors must be able to return to Iran expeditiously. That requires a return to the negotiating table."
In North Korea, where leader Kim Jong Un has a growing nuclear programme without any IAEA oversight, Mr. Grossi warned that it "stands as a stark reminder of the consequences when red lines are crossed" in violation of UN Security Council resolutions banning nuclear weapons production.
In Ukraine, he singled out the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, Europe's largest, saying it remains "in a precarious position" with frequent power losses, limited back-up diesel supplies "and military activity threatening the plant and the people who work there".
On a positive note, Mr. Grossi said the IAEA has made "significant progress" in clarifying and resolving outstanding questions regarding Syria's nuclear activities after nearly two decades of uncertainty. That is as a result of engaging with the government of interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa, he said.
He reported in September that the Bashar al-Assad-era government — which was ousted in December 2024 by opposition forces led by al-Sharaa — was constructing a nuclear reactor that was configured to produce fissile material for possible use in nuclear weapons.

briefs.headline: Shooting in Paris suburbs kills one, wounds 5 in suspected racist attack
briefs.deck: The suspect, who was arrested by police less than 20 minutes after he first started shooting, has been identified only as Kévin T, born in 1987, the National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's office said. Authorities did not disclose the man's last name
briefs.bodyText:
A gunman firing from a vehicle at three locations in the Paris suburbs killed one person and wounded at least five others, including a 12-year-old girl, in what French authorities described as a racially-motivated attack.
The suspect was arrested soon after the shooting, and France's National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's office took charge of the case. President Emmanuel Macron said it was "a racist terror attack" and that the suspect's statements suggested it was premeditated.
"These people were targeted because of their skin colour or perceived religion, and for no other reason," Mr. Macron said following a meeting with officials and residents in the suburb of Trappes, west of Paris. "There is no place for this in France."
The shootings took place over the course of about 15 minutes at three separate locations in the towns of Trappes and La Verrière, a suburban area about 30 kilometres (20 miles) from Paris, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said. One person died and five were wounded, three of them with life-threatening injuries, he said.
"A deadly rampage took place this morning," Mr. Nuñez told reporters in Trappes.
The suspect, who was arrested by police less than 20 minutes after he first started shooting, has been identified only as Kévin T, born in 1987, the National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's office said. Authorities did not disclose the man's last name.
His criminal record shows four previous convictions that had been automatically expunged under French law, the statement said.
A search of his car uncovered a Sten-type submachine gun and a canister of tear gas, and investigators found his apartment had been booby-trapped with three gas cylinders and electrical wires connected to a timer, according to the Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's office.
Another person, a member of the suspect's immediate family, also was taken into police custody during the afternoon, it said.
The National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's office said the person who died was a French man born in 2000. The medical condition of the people injured had not yet stabilised on Friday evening, it said.
Mr. Nuñez praised the five officers from the anti-crime brigade who stopped the suspect. "I commend them for their swift response," he said.
Aurore Bergé, the Minister for gender equality and fight against discriminations, said the 12-year-old girl was very seriously injured.
"If a racist motive is established, I hope that the whole nation will stand alongside the residents of Trappes, La Verrière, and the victims. We cannot tolerate even the slightest racist remark in the French Republic," she said.
Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh said the gunman appeared to have fired relatively randomly, targeting passersby at several locations including a playground, possibly because of their apparent African origin.
"This is probably one of the first attempted mass killings motivated by Islamophobia and racism," he told reporters.
The National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's office said it opened a criminal investigation into several offences, including "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise with the aggravating circumstance that the act was committed on account of the victim's actual or perceived membership of a particular race, ethnic group, nationality or religion".
The shooting happened as France braces for another day of protests against the high cost of living on Saturday (October 24, 2026), with major museums closing their doors and the government deploying a significantly larger security presence to prevent a repeat of last week's violent unrest, which shocked the country.

briefs.headline: US has for years asked Musk to alter Starlink service in Ukraine, Middle East, sources say
briefs.bodyText: Washington: Well before the throttling this month of Ukraine's military access to Elon Musk's satellite communications system, the Biden and Trump administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn its Starlink service on or off in various countries, according to six former senior US officials familiar with the matter. During the presidency of Joe Biden, the requests included switching off the service to prevent Iranian proxy militias in Yemen and Lebanon from using Starlink to communicate, and activating the service to provide internet access inside Iran and in Ukraine to support its military, said four of the former officials. .RSS affiliate Swadeshi Jagran Manch urges Centre to deny Starlink permission in India over security concerns. Similarly, President Donald Trump's administration asked Musk, who is CEO of SpaceX, to make the service available in Iran following US-Israeli strikes in 2025 and 2026, in hopes it would bolster internet access and communications for anti-government protesters, a former senior Trump official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. All of the people spoke on condition of anonymity. The previous US requests about Starlink access are being reported here for the first time. The recent blowup over restrictions to Ukraine's use of SpaceX satellite services has raised questions about the ties between the US government and Musk, whose company owns systems vital to the US military and to US allies. The Biden-era and Trump requests to Musk show a close relationship in which US administrations rely to an unprecedented degree on a private-sector company to help implement foreign policy. The recent limits on Ukraine, despite being a US ally, have also rattled officials in Europe, some of whom argue that Europe must develop its own military satellite communications capabilities because no viable short-term alternative currently exists. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last week that his country's access to Starshield, the military version of the Starlink system, had been intentionally limited, interfering with the performance of the country’s military drones. He also said the speeds were reduced for Starlink, which Ukraine uses for some military activities including defense against Russian missile attacks. Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House. The Trump administration has acknowledged the slowdown but has not said whether it gave the order. The White House, contacted for comment, referred Reuters to Trump's remarks on Friday, when he said he had not spoken with Musk about Starlink access issues for Ukraine and that "if there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out." Halyna Yusypiuk, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, said Ukraine's priority is "to have the service restored to normal speed as soon as possible, as the lives of our people depend on it." SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment, although Musk said in a social media post earlier this week: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately (by the president of the United States).” Democratic US Representative Jason Crow called on Friday for clarity about the recent changes to Ukraine's satellite service, saying there are risks to the US dependence on SpaceX. "Unelected billionaires and private corporations should not decide what is in the best interest of America's national security," Crow said. For Ukraine, the Starlink internet service has become the lifeblood of frontline communication between units, who say there is currently no rival to the capabilities of SpaceX's products. Starshield receivers, largely impervious to radio jamming, are used as onboard guidance systems and to provide links to a remote pilot for Ukrainian drones, including deep behind Russian lines inside Ukraine. Musk's role as the strong-willed CEO of a company with outsized influence over US national security has at times raised questions over who is making decisions about SpaceX's satellite services. The SpaceX CEO is "supposed to be a business executive, with government contracts, and he's essentially making huge foreign policy decisions," said Armand Musey, president of Summit Ridge Group, a satellite industry consultancy. "He's sufficiently ambiguous of a person that you don't know if his decisions are sort of his personal quirks, or it's because there's an influence elsewhere that's impacting him," Musey said. In previous years, Musk has moved to limit Ukraine’s access to Starlink. In 2022, according to Reuters reporting, Musk ordered SpaceX personnel to cut Starlink coverage in areas Ukraine was trying to retake, a move that surprised White House officials. Musk has said publicly that he refused a 2022 Ukrainian request to activate his satellite network in Crimea's port city of Sevastopol to aid an attack on Russia's fleet there, saying he feared complicity in a major act of war. The Biden administration at times relied on Musk to help implement policy, five of the former officials said. Biden officials coordinated with SpaceX to thwart US adversaries by cutting the service, and to help allies by expanding Starlink’s availability, they said. They added that discussions between the government and SpaceX, which usually included Pentagon and White House officials, often focused on preventing groups such as the Iranian-linked Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon from using Starlink terminals. Biden officials several times shared intelligence with SpaceX that indicated that the Houthis and Hezbollah were using diverted Starlink terminals — hardware that made its way to the militants through intermediaries. In October 2023, during fighting between Israel and Hezbollah militants in southern Lebanon, intelligence officials told the White House that individuals linked to Hezbollah could have gained access to Starlink terminals. Officials had similar concerns about the Houthis in Yemen in 2024 during a US air campaign against the Iran-linked group, five of the officials said. In both cases, the administration contacted SpaceX and asked it to identify the terminals and shut them off. At least some of the terminals were deactivated, said two of the officials. In a 2024 submission to the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, SpaceX said it works closely with US government agencies to secure export authorizations where required and to safeguard technology in support of US national security objectives and foreign policy goals. Soon after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Biden officials pushed SpaceX to expand Starlink use for the Ukrainian military, said two of the former officials. In a separate instance, the Biden administration asked SpaceX to turn on Starlink in Iran during a protest movement launched in September 2022 after the death of Mahsa Amini, an Iranian arrested for not wearing her hijab properly, according to one of the former officials. Starlink terminals were moved into the country with the help of the administration, said the official, who declined to say how many were transferred. .Trump says Musk restored Ukraine's Starlink access, declines to say if they spoke. The Trump administration took a similar step earlier this year and discussed with Musk and SpaceX getting Starlink terminals into Iran and activated following US-Israeli strikes in the country in June 2025 and again in February 2026, a former senior Trump official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. Neither the Trump administration nor SpaceX has publicly confirmed that those terminals were turned on. The Wall Street Journal reported in February that the US government had sent thousands of Starlink terminals into Iran. Iran's delegation to the UN did not respond to a request for comment.

briefs.headline: Judge puts off decision on Charlie Kirk murder trial date, media reports
briefs.bodyText: A Utah judge on Friday said he needed more time to decide when to start the trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing prominent right-wing activist Charlie Kirk more than a year ago, media reported. At a hearing in Provo, Utah, District Court Judge Tony Graf heard arguments from defense lawyers, prosecutors and a lawyer for Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, before saying he needed to consider their positions. He set a new hearing for November 9, television station KUTV reported. .Following in the footsteps of Charlie Kirk?. Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to seven counts, including aggravated murder, for allegedly shooting Kirk as he held one of his trademark debates at Utah Valley University in Orem. Robinson's lawyers expect a six-to-seven-month trial. Robinson's attorneys had asked for a late 2029 trial to give them time to challenge Utah's request for the death penalty, gather additional evidence and seek a change of venue, among other issues, according to a scheduling memo. Prosecutors, meanwhile, sought a date of January 31, 2028 to start what they expect to be a 17-week trial, according to their scheduling memo. In a separate filing, Erika Kirk said the defense request was "grossly out of line with comparable cases" and requested the trial start no later than October 4, 2027. Shortly before Friday's hearing, President Donald Trump, with whom Kirk had been allied, slammed Graf's handling of the case in a social media post, saying it should be tried within a month and Graf was asking "questions that people already know the answer to." Kirk was a polarizing figure in US politics. He was admired by conservatives for mobilizing young voters around his Christian and right-wing views. Opponents criticized his rhetoric on immigration, race, gender and other social issues. .Donald Trump awards Charlie Kirk Presidential Medal of Freedom month after his assassination. Prosecutors allege Robinson targeted Kirk for his opposition to gay marriage and transgender rights. Defense attorney Richard Novak has said Kirk spoke "hatefully" about people who did not have traditional gender identities or were not heterosexual, but there was no evidence Robinson opposed those views.

stories.headline: ‘Reclaim public spaces’: Civil society groups march against protest curbs
stories.deck: The protesters marched from Town Hall to challenge the Licensing and Regulation of Protests, Demonstrations and Protest Marches (Bengaluru City) Order, 2021, which the city police cite to restrict protests to Freedom Park.
stories.bodyText:
As part of a nation-wide march, civil society groups organised a Tiranga March in Bengaluru on Friday (October 23), demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR). They also called for the right to protest to be extended beyond Freedom Park.
The protesters marched from Town Hall to challenge the Licensing and Regulation of Protests, Demonstrations and Protest Marches (Bengaluru City) Order, 2021, which the city police cite to restrict protests to Freedom Park.
Apart from Town Hall, groups of protesters gathered with placards at various locations across the city, including Anandpura, Infantry Road, the War Memorial and Brigade Road.
The protesters said the march was aimed at reclaiming Town Hall and other public spaces as venues for citizens to express dissent. They demanded that the police revert to the earlier Licensing and Controlling of Assemblies and Processions (Bangalore City) Order, 2009, which they said would allow protests beyond the designated venue.
The Bengaluru City police, who have previously detained protesters for demonstrating at Town Hall, granted conditional permission for Friday’s march, restricting it to a Tiranga March and warning that participants would be detained if they displayed placards. The march was held amid a heavy police presence.

stories.headline: Karnataka’s most backward districts see low applications for inclusion after SIR draft deletions
stories.deck: In several historically backward districts, including Kalaburagi, Mysuru, Raichur and Ballari, deletions at the draft stage exceeded 18% of the electorate.
stories.bodyText:
Hearings on more than 43.82 lakh notices have been concluded, while most applications received for inclusion (Form 6), deletion (Form 7) and corrections to EPIC particulars (Form 8), filed between June 16 and September 23, the last date for filing claims and objections, have been disposed of, the office of the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) said on Friday (October 23).
The CEO’s office specified that all 58,475 Form 7 applications received during this period had been cleared on priority. The last date for disposal of claims and objections was October 22, with the final electoral roll scheduled to be published on October 27.
Most of the districts that reported high deletions under the Absent, Shifted, Dead, Duplicate and Others (ASDDO) categories during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) have received far fewer Form 6 applications seeking inclusion in the electoral rolls. The gap is particularly stark in several historically backward districts, including Kalaburagi, Mysuru, Raichur and Ballari, where deletions at the draft stage exceeded 18% of the electorate.
Source: Karnataka Chief Electoral Office
During the SIR, people whose names were excluded from the draft rolls after being marked as absent or shifted were required to file Form 6 to seek inclusion in the final electoral roll. The applications remain disproportionately low compared with the scale of deletions. Moreover, the figures do not establish how many applicants are seeking re-inclusion, as the CEO’s office has not released age-wise data or a break-up to establish how many applicants are first-time voters and how many are seeking re-inclusion.
Kalaburagi, for instance, had 23.71 lakh electors before the draft stage. A total of 5,21,957 names were deleted from the draft roll, including 47,445 people marked as absent and 3,47,606 as shifted. Against these deletions, only 44,749 Form 6 applications had been received by September 23, the cut-off date for seeking inclusion in the final roll.
Mysuru lost 19.9% of its electorate to the ASDDO list. Of its electorate of over 27.99 lakh, more than 5.57 lakh names were deleted, including 3.81 lakh people classified as absent or shifted. However, only 35,447 Form 6 applications had been received — just 6.36% of the deletions at the draft stage.
In Raichur, where 30,733 people were marked as absent and 1,87,941 as shifted, only 28,034 Form 6 applications seeking inclusion had been received. The disparity is even sharper in Ballari, where only 11,685 Form 6 applications had been received against more than 1.51 lakh people excluded — marked as shifted or absent.
Applications received after September 23 will not be reflected in the final electoral roll. Names approved for inclusion through applications filed after the cut-off date will figure in the supplementary list to be published after the final SIR rolls.
Between September 24 and October 22, more than 2.55 lakh additional Form-6 applications were filed, taking the total number of applications, filed since June 16, to over 10.42 lakh. However, even this figure remains far below the 1.07 crore names deleted at the draft stage.
Meanwhile, the number of Form 7 applications seeking deletion of names has risen sharply from 58,475 (as of September 23) to 2.28 lakh. More than 1.7 lakh applications seeking deletions were filed between September 24 and October 22.

stories.headline: Bali's cultural rhythms meet Karnataka's theatrical flair
stories.deck: Bali's cultural rhythms meet Karnataka's theatrical flair
stories.bodyText:
Bali and Bengaluru may lie thousands of kilometres apart, but they share a cultural inheritance rooted in Hindu traditions, temple rituals and the timeless epics of the 
Ramayana
 and the 
Mahabharata
. The 16-day 
Bali in Bengaluru
 festival, organised by Param Foundation, brought that connection to life through Balinese dance, puppet theatre, workshops, seminars and interactive sessions.
A landmark collaboration between Balinese performers and Karnataka’s Yakshagana artistes was at the heart of the festival, as they reimagined the 
Ramayana
 through two distinct theatrical traditions. Balinese grace and music met Yakshagana’s colourful costumes, expressive acting, spoken dialogue and rhythmic energy. From Ravana’s arrival and Sita’s abduction to Jatayu’s valiant fight and the ultimate triumph of good over evil, the performance demonstrated how an ancient story can cross borders and find fresh expression.
A tale of two traditions
For I Wayan Dibia, a Balinese dancer, choreographer and Padma Shri awardee, the connection goes beyond shared stories. “Although Bengaluru and Bali are so far away, the 
Ramayana and 
Mahabharata
 are very important in both cultures,” he says. “Around 95 per cent of Bali is Hindu,” he adds, explaining that Balinese retellings of the epics draw directly on Valmiki and Ved Vyasa.
While the stories remain familiar, their visual treatment and theatrical vocabulary differ. 
In this joint production, Sita’s graceful and measured movements convey her elegance, while Rama’s green attire, bow, and arrows establish his identity. The interplay between good and evil is central to Balinese performance. “In Bali, good and evil are understood to sit side by side rather than apart, which is why Rama and Ravana appear as paired figures on stage,” Dibia explains.
Finding Bali in Namma Bengaluru
Dibia says a traditional Balinese village has three temples dedicated to Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva. Each temple has three zones: an outer public space, a transitional middle court and an inner sanctum, which is entered only after purification. Music and dance are integrated to community life, with neither absent from Balinese rituals.
During his third visit to Bengaluru, and perhaps his ninth to India, Dibia found a familiar spiritual atmosphere in the city. “I can feel some kind of Balinese feeling here in Bengaluru, even though I cannot identify what exactly it is. The mood in India is one of prayer to God and the deities. In the morning, I hear bells, and that makes me feel at home,” he says.
When Yakshagana meets Balinese dance
At the festival, 
Ramayana
 unfolded through alternating sequences of Balinese dance and Yakshagana. The opening scenes followed the Balinese tradition, while Jatayu’s battle and the monkey warriors were presented in Yakshagana style. For Yakshagana artiste K Krishnamoorthy Thunga, who has performed across India and abroad, bringing the two forms together proved to be smoother than he had anticipated. “Art is art. There is no boundary,” he says. “Dance,” he adds, “can convey more than words, even without a common language.”
His daughter and disciple, Chithkala K Thunga, who has trained under him since 2007, points to Yakshagana’s spontaneous spoken dialogue as one of its defining features. “The headgear and ornaments are made of wood and covered in golden foil, and they are tied rather than pinned, as the 
Natya Shastra
 prescribes,” she explains. “Yakshagana’s musical ensemble relies on three key performers: the 
Bhagavata
 singer-narrator, and the 
maddale
 and 
chande
 drummers. They create the entire sound world, in contrast to the large Balinese orchestras,” she adds. Asked which role is the most challenging to portray, she says, “Sita is the most demanding role to portray as it requires a huge emotional range.”
Even the younger students are drawn to Yakshagana. Many come because of social media, and the Bali collaboration has made them even more excited. They are very excited to see what the experience will be like. Gen Z is talented, and Yakshagana can be a go-to hobby for them, or even a profession
Chithkala K Thunga, Yakshagana dancer
The collaboration between Bali and Bengaluru offered a compelling reminder that, despite differences in language, music and performance, two ancient theatrical traditions can find common ground in a shared story.

stories.headline: Ramya complains to Bengaluru Police about loud songs at 3 am
stories.deck: Ramya complains to Bengaluru Police about loud songs at 3 am
stories.bodyText:
Actor and former MP Ramya, aka Divya Spandana, has raised concerns over loud music and firecrackers during Navaratri celebrations, saying the festivities continued into the early hours of the morning. Sharing her experience of hearing the noise until 6 am, Ramya questioned the balance between celebrating festivals and respecting others’ well-being. “Even the Supreme Court has issued a ruling that prohibits the use of loud speakers between 10 pm and 6 am,” she says.
Speaking to 
Bangalore Times
, she opens up about the need for uniform rules across festivals and why celebrations must be mindful of others.
‘Rules should apply equally to all festivals’
“Whether it is New Year’s Eve, Christmas or any other festival, shouldn’t the rules apply uniformly to everyone? It shouldn’t matter who you are or what you are celebrating. There has to be a blanket rule that takes everyone’s interests into consideration. Of course, everyone has the right to celebrate, and the authorities can grant extensions for special occasions. But continuing all the way till 6 am is a bit much,” she says.
Festivals and cultural traditions are important, but our joy should not become the cause for someone else’s distress
Ramya aka Divya Spandana
Ramya says late-night celebrations can disturb senior citizens, children and others who need rest, while also affecting animals. 
She urged people to consider those who live nearby and may not be part of the festivities.
“I heard so many film songs being played for Goddess Chamundeshwari instead of 
bhakti
 songs, and they were played at full volume. Devotion should not become an excuse to play music at unearthly volumes and hours. We have the entire day, from 9 am to 10 pm, to celebrate, so let’s use that wisely,” she says.
She adds that festivals should encourage kindness and consideration, not cause distress to others.

briefs.headline: Being shunted from one lodge to another, we don’t know when we’ll get back home, say Karnataka pilgrims stranded in Jeddah
briefs.deck: The pilgrims, who were scheduled to return on October 21, have since been shuttling between the airport and lodges, with repeated cancellations leaving them unsure when they can return home or where they will stay in the meantime.
briefs.bodyText:
“We are being taken from one lodge to another in Jeddah. We don’t know who is taking us around — the airlines or the travel agents. At least 180 of us were told on October 21 that we were being taken to the airport, but we were brought to another lodge with just two rooms. There is no arrangement for food or water here,” said Afshad, one of the 600 pilgrims from Karnataka stranded in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, following flight cancellations amid escalating Houthi rebel attacks on Saudi airports and energy infrastructure.
The pilgrims, who were scheduled to return on October 21, have since been shuttling between the airport and lodges, with repeated cancellations leaving them unsure when they can return home or where they will stay in the meantime.
Elders facing issues
Many told The Hindu that they were travelling with elderly family members, some of whom have diabetes and other health conditions. With expenses mounting and food and accommodation difficult to secure, pilgrims who still had money were pooling resources to help those who could no longer afford the basics.
The pilgrims had travelled in groups from Bengaluru, Belagavi and Hubballi for Umrah on October 7. Their journeys were booked through private tour operators. With flights cancelled amid the deteriorating security situation, the pilgrims said their travel agents had left them to make their own arrangements.
24×7 Emergency Helplines:
Indian Embassy, Riyadh
Indian Consulate, Jeddah
Imran, a pilgrim from Bengaluru, said each person had paid at least ₹30,000 towards flights, food and accommodation in the last two days. With hotels full, pilgrims were asked to vacate their rooms. “We tried to take shelter at the airport, but as the crowds grew, we had to leave from there too,” he said. Mr. Imran added that a group of 40 pilgrims from Bengaluru was taken in three buses to a lodge, only to be moved again. “Some people come and tell us they are arranging our travel and take us to the airport, but we end up at one hotel or another,” he lamented.
Javed, a pilgrim from Belagavi, said the group’s return tickets on Akasa Air were cancelled on October 8. They were told that services would resume on October 20, and hence, many waited rather than spending more money on alternative tickets.
Chartered flight
When they could not get tickets on October 20, the group tried to arrange a chartered flight through Flydeal. “The travel agents told us we would be able to leave, so we went to the Jeddah airport again on October 22. But after reaching there at 2.30 a.m., we were again told that the flight had been cancelled,” Mr. Javed said.
The uncertainty continued, and the pilgrims stayed back at the airport, hoping to get seats on any operating flight. “We were told some arrangements were made and we all paid extra. Even boarding began for a flight around 3 a.m., and the luggage of a few passengers had already been loaded but even that flight was cancelled again. We could not even get our luggage back. The airline said we would get it after services resumed. We have no idea when that will happen,” a pilgrim said.
CM seeks urgent intervention
Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar has written to External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar seeking urgent intervention to facilitate the safe return of over 600 Karnataka Umrah pilgrims stranded in Makkah and Madina amid flight suspensions. He said many had exhausted their funds and were struggling to secure food and accommodation. He requested the Centre to coordinate with Saudi authorities and airlines and arrange special flights wherever necessary.

briefs.headline: Tiranga wave in Bengaluru as citizens defy barriers to rally against SIR
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: After a week’s break, a fresh wave of demonstrations against SIR hit the city Friday evening. There was a tiranga march followed by protests organised by People Against SIR, a broad alliance of organisations representing students, youngsters, farmers, workers, Dalits, adivasis, minorities and other groups.
Even before 4pm, hundreds had gathered at Puttana Chetty Town Hall from where the march was scheduled to begin till Freedom Park. Protesters chanted slogans condemning alleged police brutality against their friends in Delhi and demanded the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The chanting was, however, stopped at 4:05pm after police denied permission, clarifying that there could be no slogans or placards against Union govt or Gyanesh Kumar.
Akshay M Hakay, deputy commissioner of olice, central, announced through the microphone: “Permission for the march is conditional in nature. We were told by the organisers for a march carrying tiranga and Constitution placards, not for protests.”
Some of the participants opposed directions from police, leading to arguments. It took members of several civil society organisations to pacify sections of their own. 
“Article 19 says you can protest without arms; we are having arms it seems,” quipped Amandeep Singh, an All India Students’ Association (AISA) member.
Right before the march began, police officers scanned all the placards and collected those with messages attacking 
Election Commission of India
, Prime Minister and CM.
One such placard which questioned the CM on restrictions was torn when protester Heena refused to surrender it. A law student, Heena alleged the poster was merely about Article 19 1(a), yet police dragged her and grabbed the placard when she refused to hand it over.
Other than the initial scuffles, the participants were able to march peacefully for almost 3km with hundreds of police officers managing traffic.
With the CEO’s office stationed between Town Hall and Freedom Park, police diverted the march after a while. Organisers said despite ensuring peace, cops did not want them to pass through the CEO’s office near KR Circle. The march took a right turn near Central College and moved forward.
“We should have marched through the CEO’s office so that V Anbukkumar could also see this. Police said marchers have a tendency to raise slogans and that would have created a very embarrassing situation,” said Sitharam Gundappa, state president, Aam Aadmi Party (AAP).
“This is a cause for the country, for saving the country and bringing back the people who are disenfranchised. Since the Bihar elections, we are flagging issues with SIR... We are fighting for a democracy which has been snatched away from us...”, civic activist Tara Rao from Eddelu Karnataka rued.
IT professional Anand who had participated in India Against Corruption movement said the current circumstances are worse: “This govt is owning elections through extortion. I have protested against Congress govt before, but it was never like this.”

briefs.headline: Karnataka SIR: Teaching on the back burner
briefs.deck: Children in government and aided schools across Karnataka have not seen several of their teachers for months, for most of them have been assigned as Booth Level Officers for the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. Students tell Rishita Khanna that what initially seemed like fun with many free hours, is now making them anxious...
briefs.bodyText:
“Initially, when we were told that we had to attend only two classes a day, we were all happy. We could play, eat lunch and go home. There was no homework either. But from mid-August to September, since there were no teachers, my parents sent me to my grandparents’ home in Kolar to help with the ragi (finger millet) harvest. It has been more than a month since I last went to school. I last saw my class teacher in March,” said M. Devaraju, a class 8 student at Government Model Kannada Primary and High School in Pulikeshinagar.
With just a single teacher at this school, students from classes 5 to 8, for months, have been taking their classes together under a tree in the school playground.
Pointing to the nearly 40 children gathered there, class 7 student Ajay says the students had assumed there would be no mid-term examinations in November. “Even before the summer vacation, for months we had been attending classes like this, with four to five classes sitting together. None of us knows anything, nothing in Mathematics or Science,” he says.
For students like Devaraju and Ajay, what began as a welcome break from classes has meant months away from learning. Like them, children in government and aided schools across Karnataka have gone months without seeing their teachers, many of whom have been assigned as Booth Level Officers (BLOs) for the Election Commission of India’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls.
The SIR began in Karnataka on June 30, with the enumeration phase extended twice. The publication of the final electoral rolls, initially scheduled for October 7, has been pushed back to October 27. But teachers’ involvement in the exercise began even earlier, in May, when they were assigned pre-mapping of electoral rolls alongside their regular teaching duties.
Across Karnataka, 59,050 BLOs have been appointed for the SIR, with the Education Department contributing the largest share, followed by anganwadi workers. Neither the Chief Electoral Officer’s office nor the district administrations have disclosed a department-wise breakdown of these appointments, making it difficult to establish how many teachers have been pulled away from classrooms. However, situation from the ground suggest that several schools are now being run by a single teacher, while others have only two teachers to manage multiple classes. As per the Government Teachers Association, 70,000 people have been diverted as BLOs and BLO supervisors.
Teaching without teachers
At another school in R.T. Nagar, six of the eight teachers, including the headmaster, have been assigned BLO duties. “I asked my teacher when he would come back. He said even he didn’t know. Our attendance has also gone down. There are 22 students in our class, but more than seven do not come to school on any given day,” Preetham, a class 8 student, said, further lamenting that he had not seen his “favourite sir” for months.
With their teachers are away, Preetham and his classmates have been left to revise lessons on their own. “Most of our friends do not come and our headmaster is also not there. So, the rest of us have started bringing a football. We play, eat the mid-day meal and go home. Teachers told us to revise what they had taught us, but we do not remember what was taught. We do not know the syllabus for this year,” he said.
Series on non-teaching duties
The SIR is only the latest in a series of government exercises that have kept teachers away from classrooms.
Since the past year, teachers have been repeatedly pulled into duties unrelated to teaching, leaving them physically and mentally exhausted and with little time to do the job they were appointed for.
In September 2025, government school teachers were deployed for the Karnataka government’s Social and Educational Surve (caste survey). They then, in the remaining two months, had to rush to complete the syllabus for the 2025-26 academic year. Before they could recover lost teaching time, more than one lakh government school teachers across Karnataka, from primary to high schools, were roped in for the National Census 2027 enumeration work between April and May this year. This, for many teachers, also coincided with the evaluation of SSLC answer papers, piling one work on top of another.
Some guest teachers
The shortage is not the same across schools. While some have alloted teachers on deputation, to make up for those assigned BLO duties, Urdu- and Tamil-medium schools have scarce options because replacements must know the language of instruction.
For instance, in Kengeri, guest teachers have been assigned to several government schools to make up for staff shortage. But an Urdu-medium school in the area, which is now running with just one teacher, has no relief. With the headmaster and all secondary teachers assigned BLO duty, a primary school teacher is left to manage classes 1 to 8.
“Children come to government schools mostly because their parents cannot afford the high fees in private schools. But the government keeps putting teachers on duties other than teaching. How unfair it is on these children,” said the lone teacher, who has no experience of teaching higher classes.
A frustrated mathematics teacher at a Telugu-medium school in Shivajinagar said: “Teaching in a government school is not easy. We have to keep assuring parents that their children are learning, that teachers are coming to school. Some children do not even know the alphabet or numbers and we have to teach them from scratch. After the COVID pandemic, their learning has become even slower. We know what they need from us, but we cannot give them the time and attention they need.” She has been tied up with a string of non-teaching assignments since last Dasara.
Some BLOs say they have never faced such pressure in years of carrying out BLO or election duties. “I have been doing BLO work for 23 years, but I have never experienced this kind of risk and pressure. If the government assigns us this work, it must also take full responsibility for our safety,” a BLO said.
A BLO in the C.V. Raman Nagar Assembly constituency said she had to take her one-and-a-half-year-old daughter with her while carrying out her duties. “Even when we tell people that we will return the next day, they come out on the streets and question how we can leave. Many refuse to cooperate unless we finish the work then and there. For the last four months, the work has not stopped for even a single day. We want to return to our schools, see our students and teach them. We are worried about how they will write their SSLC examinations this time,” she said.
Centres without care
Anganwadi workers, too, have been pulled away from their regular work to serve as BLOs, leaving their centres short of staff and young children without adequate care.
An anganwadi worker in Rajagopala Nagar said her centre had 18 children aged between three and six, most of them children of labourers. She had gone door to door to identify children in this age group, including those who were about to turn three, and persuade their parents to send them to the centre. The parents were happy to know that their children would be taken care of from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
“But what assurance can we give them now?” she asked. “Only the helper is there. The children come in, she gives them milk, and they sleep there. Some play among themselves, but there is no one to look after them properly or teach them alphabets and numbers, get them to write, and engage them in activities.”
Verifying beneficiaries
Alongside their work at anganwadi centres and their BLO duties, workers have also been tasked with verifying beneficiaries of the State government’s Gruha Lakshmi scheme, which provides ₹2,000 a month to the woman head of an eligible household. The work involves checking beneficiaries’ details, following up on delayed payments, and collecting or uploading documents for verification. “All that work has come to a standstill in between. Those people need us, but we could not assist them, and again complaints go against us. They think we are deliberately avoiding them or discriminating against them,” Lakshmi said.
Even as this work piled up, anganwadi workers were also assigned polio-related duties, requiring them to go door to door. “Even then, calls would come from the BLO supervisor asking why our progress had been low on certain days. How much work can one person do?” Lakshmi asked.
The strain has also left the anganwadi helpers, who are expected to keep the centres running in the workers’ absence, struggling with responsibilities they are not accustomed to handling.
Helpers said maintaining food-count registers, recording entries, checking expiry dates of supplies, and keeping records were tasks handled by the workers. “What will happen if someone comes and asks us about these records?” one helper questioned, arguing that the government should not introduce schemes and these activities at the cost of anything that involves children.
Same pay, unequal work
From enumeration phase, till delivering notices, making additions to the rolls, and assisting voters, BLOs are paid only an annual remuneration of ₹12,000 annually, which the Election Commission of India doubled only this year. But the amount remains the same regardless of how many people a BLO is responsible for, even as the workload differs sharply from one area to another. “Every area has a different population. A BLO handling 1,200 people gets the same remuneration as one handling 400. If the payment cannot be calculated per person, there should at least be an additional incentive beyond a certain number,” a BLO argued.
Teachers’ associations have repeatedly written to the Education Department, seeking exemption from non-teaching duties, but their demands have gone unheeded. The Government Primary School Teachers’ Association also wrote to the department and the Chief Electoral Officer shortly before the publication of the draft electoral rolls, requesting teachers not be assigned after the draft rolls phase. Anganwadi workers, too, had staged protests for days before the SIR began, demanding that they be relieved of BLO duties.
However, on August 19, the Deputy Commissioner’s office issued another order extending BLO duties until the publication of the final electoral rolls.
Proposed safeguard
The repeated diversion of teachers from classrooms has recently prompted a proposed legislative change that would make teachers the last resort for non-teaching duties, including election work and census exercises. A draft of the legislation has been circulated among government departments for their concurrence.
Under the proposed framework, district administrations would have to first prepare a register of non-teaching personnel available across government departments, statutory boards, corporations and public sector undertakings. Retired public servants and trained volunteers would also be included. These personnel would have to be fully utilised before teachers could be considered for such duties.
A teacher could be deployed only after the jurisdictional Deputy Commissioner certifies that no other personnel are available. The requisition and the certificate would have to be routed through the district education office to the Block Education Officer or Deputy Director.
However, officials from the Education Department said that unless vacancies across government departments, including the Education Department, are filled, teachers may continue to be assigned non-teaching duties because they are the largest pool of government employees.
